evals.name: the-id-comes-from-the-path
evals.prompt: In the Ktor server at {fixture}, add an endpoint that changes a note: the client sends the whole Note as the body to the note's address. Add what the port and the route need, and the tests you would write (as code; do not build, there is no Gradle wrapper). The storage implementation is somebody else's task: write the port's signature and say what its filter must be.
evals.expected_output: A typed PATCH (or PUT) on NoteResource.ById whose write is addressed by the path's id and the caller's id, never by the id in the body; one answer for a note that is not the caller's and one that does not exist; a test for exactly that.
expectations: The route is registered with the typed resource (patch<NoteResource.ById> or put<NoteResource.ById>), not with a string path
The note that is written takes its id from the path (for example `.copy(id = path.id)`), and the id in the request body is ignored or overwritten
The new port method takes the owner's id as a parameter, and the answer says the storage filter must include the owner as well as the id
A note that belongs to somebody else and a note that does not exist get the same status
There is a test in which a caller sends their own note's address with another user's note id in the body, and it asserts the other user's note is unchanged
The caller's id comes from withUser, not from the body or a header read in the handler
The answer does not add `authenticate` inside noteRouting

evals.name: a-defaulted-lambda-under-singleOf
evals.prompt: In the server at {fixture}, CreateOrderUseCase generates its ids with UUID.randomUUID() inside invoke, so a test cannot predict them. Make the id source a constructor parameter that production does not have to supply. Change whatever else has to change with it, and say what you checked. Do not build; there is no Gradle wrapper.
evals.expected_output: The parameter is added with a default; the Koin registration becomes an explicit lambda because singleOf would ask the container for a Function0; the graph test gains a resolution by type, since verify() does not see a defaulted parameter.
expectations: CreateOrderUseCase takes the id source as a constructor parameter with a default (for example `ids: () -> String = { UUID.randomUUID().toString() }`)
The registration in orderModule is no longer singleOf(::CreateOrderUseCase): it is an explicit lambda such as `single { CreateOrderUseCase(get()) }`

The answer says why: singleOf resolves every constructor parameter, defaults included, so the default would become a request to the container for a function type and fail on first use, not at start-up

The graph test gains a check that resolves CreateOrderUseCase by type from a koinApplication (koin.get<CreateOrderUseCase>() or equivalent) with a stub for the repository, rather than relying on verify() alone
The answer states that verify() does not catch a missing binding for a parameter that has a default
runCatching in the suspend invoke is replaced by a variant that rethrows CancellationException, or the answer points it out

evals.name: a-worker-on-two-replicas
evals.prompt: The service at {fixture} runs as one pod and went down during a node drain last week. Change it to run as two replicas. Make every change that needs making, in the code and in charts/app/values.yaml, and list what you verified and what somebody still has to verify on a real cluster. Do not build; there is no Gradle wrapper.
evals.expected_output: The replica count is not the only change: the outbox relay has no claim on its rows and would publish every row twice, so it gets a claim or runs on an elected leader; the connection count is checked against the database's limit; concurrent migration at start is addressed; the relay's stop joins.
expectations: The answer identifies that OutboxRelay, started in every process, would publish each outbox row once per replica

The relay is changed so that only one replica publishes a given row: a claim in the database (for example `for update skip locked` inside a transaction, or an optimistic status update) or a leader election, and the answer says which and why
The connection budget is computed: two replicas plus the extra one during a rolling deploy, times a pool of 40, against 100 connections — and the pool size or the replica count is changed so it fits
The answer addresses two replicas starting at once and migrating: Flyway's own lock, or migrating in a separate step before the pods start
values.yaml is not changed to `replicas: 2` alone with everything else left as it was
The relay's stop() waits for its loop (cancelAndJoin or equivalent), or the answer points out that stop() only cancels
The answer lists, as not verified here, a real two-replica run in which no row is published twice — it does not claim that was tested
